concepts.heading: Relationships as Living Agreements, Not Static Contracts
concepts.alt: Two guides signing a scroll together that has a small plant growing from it
concepts.plain: A relationship is an agreement you keep updating, not a contract signed once.

concepts.heading: The Three Elements of a Healthy Relationship Agreement
concepts.alt: A guide juggling three coloured balls marked with a flame, a little fence and a heart
concepts.plain: A healthy agreement has three parts: desires, boundaries and truth.

concepts.heading: 1. The Desire Element
concepts.alt: A guide holding a glowing wish star in cupped hands
concepts.plain: Everyone has wants beyond the basic commitment. Say them out loud.

concepts.heading: 2. The Boundary Element
concepts.alt: A guide standing beside an open, welcoming garden gate
concepts.plain: Boundaries are not walls. They are limits you agree on together.

concepts.heading: 3. The Truth Element
concepts.alt: A guide holding a clear glass heart up to the light
concepts.plain: Be fully honest about all of it.

checks.prompt: How does the lesson describe boundaries?
checks.explanation: They are not walls. Boundaries are not walls. Boundaries are agreements about what is and isn't okay with you.

checks.prompt: What are the three elements of a healthy relationship agreement?
checks.explanation: Desire, boundary and truth. Nelson's framework covers desires, boundaries and truth, with radical honesty across all three.

8f065bda-c879-442f-a12c-ecd593103a92.takeaway: A relationship is a living agreement. Talk about desires, limits and the truth, and keep updating it.

concepts.heading: Infidelity as Symptom
concepts.alt: A guide holding a wrench and looking at a cracked heart-shaped gauge
concepts.plain: Cheating is often a sign of unmet needs, not a random betrayal. It still hurts.

concepts.heading: The Erotic Recovery Process
concepts.alt: Carefully rebuilding a small bridge between them, plank by plank
concepts.plain: After a betrayal, trust is rebuilt in steps.

concepts.heading: Regular Renegotiation: The Key to Longevity
concepts.alt: A guide adding a heart sticker to a wall calendar
concepts.plain: Every agreement needs to be revisited on a regular basis.

options: As a symptom of unmet needs within the agreement
checks.explanation: As a symptom of unmet needs within the agreement. Nelson reframes infidelity not as random betrayal, but as a symptom of unmet needs within the relationship agreement.

checks.after: Regular Renegotiation: The Key to Longevity
checks.prompt: What is the key to longevity?
checks.explanation: Regular renegotiation. Nelson emphasizes that all agreements need regular renegotiation.

6568f55f-d1f2-45fb-8065-6ea66e414c76.takeaway: An affair usually points to needs the agreement was not meeting. Agreements need regular updates.

concepts.heading: Sexual Frequency and Satisfaction
concepts.alt: Cuddled contentedly on a sofa under a blanket
concepts.plain: Researchers have studied what keeps couples satisfied over the long run.

concepts.heading: The New Monogamy is Not Just About Sex
concepts.alt: A guide holding a basket containing a little house, a coin, a clock and a heart
concepts.plain: These agreements cover the whole relationship, not only sex.

concepts.heading: Navigating Jealousy in Redesigned Relationships
concepts.alt: Calmly holding a lantern with a small green flame inside
concepts.plain: Jealousy shows up in every kind of relationship. It is normal.

concepts.heading: Boundary Renegotiation
concepts.alt: Two guides redrawing a chalk line on the ground together
concepts.plain: As you change, your agreements have to change too.

concepts.heading: Managing External Social Pressure
concepts.alt: A guide walking calmly past a group of whispering silhouettes
concepts.plain: Friends and family will have opinions. You do not have to take them on.

checks.after: The New Monogamy is Not Just About Sex
checks.prompt: The New Monogamy framework applies to…
options: All relationship agreements, not just sexual ones
checks.explanation: All relationship agreements, not just sexual ones. The framework applies to all relationship agreements, not just sexual agreements.
Because relationships evolve. Relationships evolve, and so must agreements.

cda27767-a3f4-4833-90e9-1c327995d764.takeaway: Jealousy, changing needs and other people's opinions are normal challenges. Talk and renegotiate.

concepts.heading: Designing Your Own Relationship Agreement
concepts.alt: Two guides writing on one shared sheet of paper at a table
concepts.plain: Write your agreement down, starting with what you are committed to.

concepts.heading: The Transformation
concepts.alt: Two guides stepping out of fog into sunlight, holding hands
concepts.plain: Spelling things out instead of assuming changes a relationship for the better.

concepts.heading: The Art of Regular Check-Ins
concepts.alt: A guide sitting with a notebook and two cups, a small calendar beside her
concepts.plain: The couples who do best have regular, planned check-ins.

concepts.heading: Evolving Together Over Time
concepts.alt: A guide looking at a row of six hourglasses
concepts.plain: The average couple waits six years to get help. Do not wait.

concepts.heading: Resources for Continued Growth
concepts.plain: Books and workshops can help you keep growing.

checks.prompt: What practice do the most successful redesigned relationships share?
checks.explanation: Regular, structured check-ins. The most successful redesigned relationships share one practice: regular, structured check-ins.

checks.prompt: How long does the average couple wait before seeking help?
checks.explanation: 6 years. Dr. John Gottman's research shows that the average couple waits 6 years before seeking help for relationship problems.

60c7c403-4d99-43a7-800e-fef3136b171f.takeaway: Write your agreement down, check in on a schedule, and get help early instead of waiting years.
